near_miss.lead: ON orð ... á munni (word in the mouth) ~ Lat. mentum/uerbum
near_miss.why_not: Skaldic 'words came to Egil's mouth' vs a Plautine catalogue of face parts (mentum 'chin'); no shared collocation; munnr~mentum cognacy is real but contexts unrelated.

near_miss.lead: heriaði til frǫgðar sér ok ríkis (raided for fame and power)
near_miss.why_not: Fame motive is present in ON but frægð is not cognate with any fame word in the partner; Herodotus passage (Amasis and Ladike) unrelated.
Only shared roots in narrative prose (koma ~ βαίνω, konungr ~ γένος); no collocation.

near_miss.lead: ernir ok hrafnar on every ship-prow (beasts of battle omen)
near_miss.why_not: Beasts-of-battle is a Germanic (ON/OE) motif; partners are Solon's olbos speech and a Herodotean voyage; no cross-branch cognate wording.

near_miss.lead: báru ... orð til konungs (bear words to the king) ~ Lat. fero
near_miss.why_not: Latin partners have fero with aqua/fructum, not with verba; 'carry a message' is generic; no cross-branch instance found in slab.

near_miss.lead: lie down to sleep in the night: ON í nótt ... at sofa ... lagði ~ Russ. Легъ ... спать на темную ночь
near_miss.why_not: Cognates nátt~ночь, sofa~спать, leggja~лечь, but the ON verb is leggja 'lay' (object), not reflexive 'lie down'; 'lie down to sleep at night' is everyday language and the byline is late; chance cannot be excluded.

near_miss.lead: kinship lists: mother/wife/sister (Ir. a mathair ⁊ a mnái ⁊ a siair ~ ORuss. сестры ... мт҃ре и жены), father and mother pairs
near_miss.why_not: All inherited kin terms, but listing kin is generic; the Irish is Alexander/Darius matter translated from Latin, the ORuss. is chronicle prose; no fixed order or figure shared.

near_miss.lead: Fyrr skal hverr várr falla um þveran annan en flýja ('each shall fall across another before fleeing')
near_miss.why_not: 'Die rather than flee' is a universal heroic topos (also OE Maldon, same branch); Greek partners describe a rout and a night message, not the vow; falla/flýja have no cognate counterpart in them.

near_miss.lead: fóru dag ok nótt (travelled day and night)
near_miss.why_not: Day-and-night merism is generic; Homer partner has only ἐν νυκτί 'born in one night'; not the same collocation.

near_miss.lead: sætt var eiðum bundin / bundit einkamálum (treaty bound with oaths) ~ Skt. satyasaṃdha, bandhu; hefi ek heyrt ~ Lat. audies
near_miss.why_not: 'Bind an agreement' is metaphorically widespread (Hitt. išḫiul is a non-cognate parallel); MBh satya-saṃdha is 'true to promise', bandhu-jana 'kinsfolk' — not the binding of a treaty; Cato's ear remedy is irrelevant to the skaldic 'I have heard'.

near_miss.lead: fáum aldri svefn eða ró í nátt (we get no sleep tonight) ~ Lat. hac nocte in somnis ~ AV svapna
near_miss.why_not: Cognate sleep/night words in unrelated contexts (complaint of noise vs dream report vs charm to Sleep); generic.

near_miss.lead: troll-woman reddens the wolf's mouth with blood (ulfs munn litar ... blóði)
near_miss.why_not: Feeding the wolf is a Germanic kenning/battle motif; partner is Thucydidean treaty prose; nothing cross-branch.

near_miss.lead: heart in the breast: ON brióst ... konungs hiarta ~ OIr. a chridi 'na chlíab
near_miss.why_not: ON is about the king's unflinching heart (courage), Irish is the Táin wound formula (spear through shield, three ribs, heart in his chest); only hiarta~cride cognate, clíab not cognate with brióst; anatomical language, not a shared figure.

near_miss.lead: night grows murky: ON um nóttina er myrkt var orðit / myrkt af nótt ~ Serb. мркла ноћ, ноћи ... мрака; also ORuss. Igor Tale Длъго ночь мрькнетъ (orv spi 33) and ON er nótt myrkþi (AM-35-fol 237)
near_miss.why_not: Both members are cognate (*mergʷ- + *nókʷts) and the pairing is formulaic in both traditions (saga 'myrkt af nótt', Serbian epic 'мркла ноћ', 'од јутра до мрака'), but the root's meaning 'dark' makes 'the night darkens' predictable everyday language; the root is only North European (Gmc, BSl), so this is at most a lexical isogloss, not demonstrable inherited phraseology.

near_miss.lead: mǫrg eru konungs eyru ('many are the king's ears')
near_miss.why_not: Slab partner is unrelated (stormy night off Euboea); see search lead: the Greek parallel is about the Persian king's 'eyes and ears' and is best taken as a diffused topos, not inherited.

search_lead.cognate: ON eyra ~ Gk οὖς (*h₂ṓws); konungr and βασιλεύς not cognate; margr ~ πολύς renewed
search_lead.argument: ON proverb 'many are the king's ears' (also Jómsvíkinga saga, with 'sem mælt er') and 'eyes and ears to the king' correspond to the Greek report that the Persian king 'has many ears and many eyes' (Xenophon, Cyropaedia 8.2.10-12, not found in the local corpus; the corpus has only Herodotus' and Aristophanes' 'King's Eye'). Likely a learned or Iranian-derived topos (cf. Mithra's thousand ears, Varuṇa's spies) rather than inherited wording; offered for review only.

note: Second reading of 22 flagged bundles; no claims: all leads generic (kin lists, sleep/night, die-rather-than-flee) or partner-unrelated; 'night grows murky' (*mergʷ- + *nókʷts, ON~Serb~ORuss) recorded as near-miss; 'many are the king's ears' as search lead.
